stories.headline: DOW TOPS 50,000 WHILE S&P, NASDAQ SLIP AS NVIDIA GIVES BACK CHUNK OF MONDAY'S HUANG-REINSTATEMENT RALLY
stories.body: The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed roughly 420 points to close above 50,000, even as the S&P 500 fell 0.49% to 7,201 — its eighth loss in nine sessions — and the Nasdaq 100 dropped 1.99% to 26,214, after Nvidia and other chip and AI-server names surrendered a large share of Monday's reinstatement-driven surge.
stories.explain: The split is a direct consequence of how the three gauges are built: the Dow is price-weighted and dominated by high-dollar, non-tech names, so it can rally on strength in names like UnitedHealth even while the cap-weighted S&P and Nasdaq 100 — both heavily loaded with Nvidia and its AI-supply-chain peers — get dragged down when that single sector reverses. Today's reversal shows how fragile Monday's rally was: a move built on one stock's ~30% one-day gain unwinds just as mechanically as it built, which is why the eighth S&P loss in nine sessions matters more for the broad market than one good Monday did.

stories.headline: SANOFI AGREES TO BUY INSMED IN MULTIBILLION-DOLLAR DEAL, LIFTING HEALTH CARE TO TOP OF THE DOW
stories.body: Sanofi announced a formal agreement to acquire Insmed, picking up the recently approved lung-disease drug Brinsupri and the inhaled antibiotic Arikayce, in a deal reported in the tens of billions of dollars that followed a week of takeover speculation; the news pushed health-care stocks to the top of the sector leaderboard and helped offset the chip-sector drag on the broader market.
stories.explain: A pharma company paying a large premium for a single approved asset plus a late-stage pipeline (treprostinil palmitil inhalation powder) signals that strategic buyers see more value in buying proven respiratory-drug revenue than building it internally — a classic build-versus-buy calculus that compresses when a drugmaker like Sanofi faces its own patent-cliff pressure on Dupixent. Because UnitedHealth, Merck and Amgen are among the Dow's highest-priced components, health-care sector strength has an outsized, mechanical lift on the price-weighted Dow relative to its effect on the cap-weighted S&P 500, which is one reason the two benchmarks diverged today.

stories.headline: DECEMBER HIKE ODDS HOLD NEAR 75-80% WITH TOMORROW'S CORE PCE THE LAST DATA CHECK BEFORE THE FED MEETS
stories.body: Futures markets continue to price roughly a three-in-four chance of a quarter-point hike at the December 9 FOMC meeting, with the fed funds rate still at 3.75%-4.00%; October core PCE — the Fed's preferred inflation gauge — is due Wednesday morning, pulled forward a day ahead of Thursday's Thanksgiving holiday, making it the last major data point before the committee meets.
stories.explain: Core PCE strips out volatile food and energy prices and adjusts for consumers substituting toward cheaper goods, giving the Fed a cleaner read on underlying price pressure than CPI — which is why a single print carries this much weight going into a meeting where odds are already skewed toward a hike. A hotter-than-expected number would likely cement those odds further and pressure both stocks and bonds into the holiday, while a soft read is the market's last realistic chance to unwind some of the hike pricing before the Fed's blackout period begins.

stories.headline: OIL EXTENDS GAINS TO $82 ON HORMUZ DISRUPTION AS GOLD AND THE DOLLAR BOTH RETREAT
stories.body: WTI crude rose 2.64% to around $82 a barrel as continued tanker disruptions tied to the US-Iran conflict around the Strait of Hormuz kept a floor under prices, while gold fell 2.08% to roughly $3,555 an ounce and the dollar index slipped 0.42% to 103.84.
stories.explain: Oil trading on its own supply-disruption premium even as equities see a risk-off day shows crude pricing a geopolitical chokepoint risk independently of the broader macro tape, since a closed or contested Strait of Hormuz removes real barrels from the market regardless of what the Fed or AI stocks are doing. Gold and the dollar falling together is the more conventional pairing breaking down in reverse of Monday's pattern, consistent with investors unwinding some of last week's safe-haven positioning now that the immediate Nvidia-leadership shock has passed, even as the Hormuz risk underneath oil has not.

stories.headline: HUANG'S DEC. 1 TESTIMONY AS A SITTING CEO STAYS THE KEY RISK EVENT AFTER TODAY'S PULLBACK
stories.body: With Nvidia shares giving back roughly a fifth of Monday's gain, attention is turning to Jensen Huang's December 1 closed-door testimony before the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence, and China select committees — now delivered as a reinstated, sitting CEO rather than a departed executive — with general counsel Tim Teter following December 2.
stories.explain: A sitting CEO testifying on national-security-adjacent matters faces a materially higher bar than a former one, since lawmakers can press him directly on current supply-chain and China-exposure decisions rather than just the circumstances of his earlier resignation. Today's pullback suggests the market is already starting to price that event risk back in after Monday's relief rally, which is why Nvidia's reaction into December 1 — not just this week's chip-sector moves — is the cleaner signal of whether the governance overhang has actually been resolved.

watchlist: Oct. core PCE inflation — Wed., Nov. 25, 8:30 AM ET, released a day early ahead of Thanksgiving and the last major print before the Fed's Dec. 9 meeting
Jensen Huang's closed-door House testimony — Dec. 1, now as a sitting CEO, with GC Tim Teter following Dec. 2
Fed's Dec. 9 FOMC decision — hike odds near 75-80% with the funds rate at 3.75%-4.00%
Nvidia and chip-sector follow-through — shares gave back a chunk of Monday's ~30% reinstatement rally; watch whether the pullback extends
Sanofi-Insmed deal close and financing details — health-care M&A that lifted the Dow even as the S&P and Nasdaq fell

deepDive.title: Why the Dow Can Rise While the S&P and Nasdaq Fall: Price-Weighting vs. Cap-Weighting
content: Today's tape handed finance students a clean, real-time example of something textbooks usually only describe in the abstract: three major U.S. indexes moving in different directions on the same day, for mechanical reasons tied entirely to how each one is built. The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed above 50,000, while the S&P 500 fell 0.49% and the Nasdaq 100 dropped 1.99%, as Nvidia and its AI-supply-chain peers gave back a chunk of Monday's reinstatement-driven surge and Sanofi's acquisition of Insmed lifted health-care stocks. The divergence isn't noise — it's the direct, calculable output of two fundamentally different index construction methods colliding with a day that had both an AI-stock pullback and a health-care-sector lift.

The Dow is price-weighted, a methodology dating to 1896 when Charles Dow simply averaged the share prices of his original 12 components. That means a stock's influence on the index depends only on its dollar price per share, not on the company's market capitalization. UnitedHealth, trading in the several-hundred-dollar range, moves the Dow far more per percentage point than a similarly-sized company trading at $50. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100, by contrast, are float-adjusted market-cap-weighted: a stock's influence depends on the total value of its tradable shares, which is why Nvidia — a roughly $3-4 trillion company — can single-handedly move those two indexes by several percentage points, as it did both up on Monday and down today, while barely registering in the Dow, where it isn't even the highest-priced component.

What gets missed is that price-weighting is a historical accident that nobody would design from scratch today, yet it persists because changing it would break decades of continuity in the most quoted index in financial media. The clearest illustration is Apple's 7-for-1 stock split in 2014: despite no change in the company's market value, Apple's Dow weighting collapsed overnight simply because its share price dropped from about $650 to under $100, while its actual economic importance to the index was unchanged. That same mechanical quirk is why healthcare's gain today — driven by high-priced names like UnitedHealth and Merck — could lift the Dow even as the broader, cap-weighted market fell on an AI-sector reversal worth far more in absolute dollar terms.

For a market setup heading into Wednesday's core PCE print and the Fed's December 9 decision, the lesson is practical, not just historical: headline index levels can mask what's actually driving returns. A student reading only 'the Dow hit a record' today would miss that the broader, more economically representative market actually fell, and that the move was concentrated in two unrelated stories — an AI-leadership reversal and a pharma acquisition — rather than a shift in the macro outlook. That distinction matters directly for how to read tomorrow's PCE reaction: if core inflation surprises and only the Dow's relatively tech-light composition cushions the hit, that will say more about index construction than about the economy.
